Brand book · Edition 2

Every ingredient has an address.

Lavané is a kitchen that starts with the basics: stone-milled flour, slow-churned ghee, honest salt, and vegetables from growers we can name. With them we cook modern European and Indian food. The kitchen is vegetarian, and it doesn't need to shout about it.

The landscape

What the best vegetarian and ingredient-led kitchens already know

We studied vegetarian restaurants from Bengaluru to Vienna, plus brands that built their identity around ingredients and craft, from a Paris bakery to a Pune ghee maker.

Placed by our own reading of two questions: whose table does the kitchen cook for, Indian or European, and how much does it build its story on where ingredients come from?

Restaurant or food brand studied
Not vegetarian, studied for its ingredient story
Where Lavané aims to stand

Kitchens that build everything around ingredients tend to cook European food, like Blue Hill, TIAN and Poilâne. Indian vegetarian chains are loved for taste and trust but rarely talk about where their flour or ghee comes from. Indian ingredient brands such as Two Brothers tell the origin story beautifully, but they sell groceries, not dinner. Nobody yet cooks European and Indian food from named Indian basics. That is Lavané's space.

Vegetarian is normal in India

Pew found 39% of Indian adults call themselves vegetarian. It doesn't need a banner. A small, familiar sign is enough.

Pew Research Center, 2021
!

“Organic” has rules

Under EU rules, hydroponic produce cannot be sold as organic. Lavané says “organic” or “hydroponic” for each item, and never blurs the two.

Regulation (EU) 2018/848
?

Describe the method, not the label

India's food regulator ordered A1/A2 labels off dairy in 2024, then withdrew the order days later. Describing the method, “bilona, from cultured curd”, is clearer and harder to dispute.

FSSAI, August 2024
2
How the others look

Four ways food brands sign their name

Looking at logos across this space, most fall into four families. Lavané's first logo, the leaf, sat in the most crowded one.

The green leaf

Used by countless vegetarian, organic and health brands. It says “healthy”, not “delicious”, and it is impossible to own.

Lavané moves away from it

The heritage emblem

Crests, gods, temples and founders' portraits. Common among Indian vegetarian chains. Builds trust, but looks regional and dated abroad.

We borrow the trust, not the look

The friendly wordmark

Lowercase, rounded and modern, as sweetgreen and many Swiss and UK chains do. Clean, but interchangeable.

Too anonymous for a story this rich

The maker's mark

A stamp that goes on the product itself, like the letter Poilâne presses into every loaf. It proves who made the food.

3
Where we stand

Lavané in one sentence

For people who want to know what they are eating, Lavané is the kitchen that starts at the root: stone-milled flour, slow-churned ghee, honest salt and vegetables we can trace, cooked into modern European and Indian food.

Guest one
“I read labels. I want to know where my flour and ghee come from.”

Careful eaters, often parents, who shop organic at home and rarely find a restaurant that matches.

Guest two
“I just want a seriously good pasta. Oh, it's vegetarian? Didn't notice.”

Food lovers who come for flavour. For them, vegetarian should feel like a detail, not a theme.

Guest three
“This tastes like my grandmother's ghee, in a dish I've never had.”

People raised on Indian home cooking who want those roots in a modern, European setting.

Lavané is
  • Obsessed with basics: flour, ghee, salt, oil, water
  • Traceable: every key ingredient has a source we can name
  • Rooted: old Indian methods like the stone mill, bilona and wood press
  • Modern on the plate: European technique, Indian memory
Lavané is not
  • A “pure veg” sign. The kitchen is vegetarian, and we say so quietly.
  • A health brand. No calorie counts, no superfood claims.
  • Vague. No “natural” or “farm-fresh” without proof.
  • Nostalgic only. The roots are old, the cooking is new.

What we believe

Six house beliefs

लवणेन भोज्यम् lavaṇena bhojyam

“With salt, food becomes worth eating.” If the simplest ingredient can make or ruin a meal, then every ingredient matters. That is the whole philosophy.

Start with the basics

Flour, ghee, salt and oil are in almost everything. They deserve the most care, not the least.

Flour is stone-milled every week; ghee is churned the bilona way; oils are wood-pressed.

Every ingredient has an address

If we can't say where something came from, it doesn't go on the plate.

An origin card on every table, and named growers on the menu.

Back to the roots

The old ways were often the better ways: the stone chakki, the bilona churn, the wooden press.

A working stone mill in the dining room.

Grown honestly

Organic, soil-grown when we can. Clean hydroponic when that's better. Always labelled as which.

Each vegetable on the origin card says “organic” or “hydroponic”.

A kitchen you can see into

Hygiene isn't a certificate on the wall. It's something guests can watch.

An open kitchen, and the latest hygiene inspection result posted at the door.

Old roots, new plates

Khapli wheat becomes tagliatelle. Ghee finishes a risotto. The ingredients are Indian, and the cooking goes anywhere.

Every season brings one dish that crosses between the two kitchens.
5
The ingredient standard

What we promise about the basics

This replaces a “pure veg” sign. It is specific, checkable and printed on the origin card.

FlourWhole grains, including heritage wheat like khapli, stone-milled in small batches and used within days.
GheeBilona method: curd from whole milk, hand-churned to butter, slowly simmered. Milk from named dairies.
SaltUnrefined sea salt and rock salt. Named on the menu, like Poilâne names Guérande.
OilsWood-pressed (kachi ghani) and cold-pressed. Never refined oils.
VegetablesCertified organic and soil-grown, or hydroponic from named farms. Every item labelled with which one it is.
HygieneAn open kitchen and daily checklists, with the latest inspection result displayed at the door.
VegetarianOur kitchen has never cooked meat or fish. Said once, quietly, at the bottom of the menu.
Two cautions: under EU law, hydroponic produce can't be sold as organic, so always label the two separately. And describe ghee by its method rather than with “A2” claims: India's regulator tried to remove those labels in 2024, then withdrew the order.

7
The mark

Five bold routes from the ingredient story

Each route turns one part of the story into a mark. All of them use Gloock, a sharp, high-contrast serif that feels like a Paris bistro sign, with the crystal accent kept from the first logo.

Top pick

The Chakki

A stone millstone, drawn with the grooves real millers cut, and a grain of salt in its eye. It is set inside a square, so to anyone in India it also reads like the familiar green vegetarian mark: a circle inside a square. To guests in Europe it is simply a miller's stamp.

Why it wins: it carries the hook (flour, roots, process) and the salt from the verse. It signals vegetarian without saying a word, and it works as a stamp pressed into bread, a brass coin and a 16-pixel app icon.

The Ingredient Table

Lavané as element La, with every basic as its own tile: At for atta, Gh for ghee, Na for salt. A whole labelling system for menus and packaging.

Use as: the menu icon system alongside the Chakki.

The Roots

A sprout above, roots below, and the wordmark as the soil line between them. “Back to the roots”, taken literally.

Use as: the growers' programme and the farm-partner badge.

Slow Churn

A drop of ghee with the bilona's spiral turning inside it. Hypnotic, warm, and instantly ghee.

Use as: the ghee jar and anything sold to take home.

The Atta Sack

The stencil printed on flour sacks in European mills and Indian chakkis alike. Raw, industrial and honest.

Use as: packaging, aprons, crates and the delivery bag.

The identity

A miller's stamp, a bistro wordmark

The Chakki leads, the four other routes each have a clear job, and the palette moves from leafy green to the colours of the ingredients: flour, stone, ghee and soil. Green appears only where it means vegetarian.

Primary logo

The Chakki, the wordmark and “Vegetarian Kitchen”, set small. Use it on signage, menus and the website.

Reversed on stone

For the fascia, uniforms and dark packaging.

Horizontal

For website headers, receipts and narrow signs.

Devanagari

लवणे · शाकाहारी रसोई (“vegetarian kitchen”), for Indian signage alongside the primary logo.

With the verse

Grown, milled, churned, cooked, with the verse beneath. For the entrance and the first page of the menu.

The Chakki alone

For the bread stamp, app icon, wax seal and embossing.

Ingredient tiles

For marking the basics on the menu and on labels.

Rituals

Things guests will tell their friends about

Six habits that turn the ingredient story into something people can see, smell and taste.

Every morning

The milling hour

A working stone mill in the window grinds the day's flour, with the smell of fresh atta drifting out onto the street.

On arrival

The first pinch

Warm bread, a spoon of fresh ghee and a pinch of named salt arrive before anything else. The verse, served.

On every table

The origin card

Where today's flour, ghee, greens, roots and salt came from. It changes daily.

On the bread

The maker's mark

The Chakki is pressed into every house loaf and stamped on the ghee seal. The food carries its own signature.

Every Sunday

Churning day

Ghee is churned in the open kitchen. Guests can watch, taste, and take a jar home.

Every week

The growers' board

A chalkboard of this week's farms and millers, beside the names of the cooks on shift.

In the world

The mark on real things

Bread, ghee, flour sacks, stone and paper. The identity looks best on the ingredients themselves.

·
Next steps and sources

Before this book goes to print

Find the suppliers first. The brand promises named flour, ghee and greens. Sign the first mills, dairies and farms before launch.
Check the veg-mark echo. The Chakki echoes India's vegetarian symbol. Ask a food-law adviser before using it on packaged food, where that symbol is regulated.
Refine the wordmark. Have a type designer customise the Gloock wordmark so it is fully yours before filing a trademark.
Check every claim. Organic, hydroponic and ghee claims must match the rules in each market you open in.
